# Index Fund Basics

## Overview

I began buying index funds in 2016 after watching actively managed funds trail their benchmarks year after year. The logic is simple: own a slice of an entire market rather than betting on a handful of stocks. Accumulation is the slow part. I set a monthly transfer and let it run, adding extra when a bonus lands. Diversification carries the heavy load, because a broad fund holds hundreds or thousands of companies and one bad earnings report barely moves the balance. Tracking error is the gap between a fund's return and its index, and a well-run fund keeps that gap to a few basis points. I care about that figure more than about a flashy one-year return, since the gap is what I actually pay for the wrapper.

## Choosing a Fund

When I pick a fund, the first thing I check is what index it actually tracks. Two funds can both say global equity and still hold very different things: one tracks the MSCI World, which is developed markets only, and the other tracks the FTSE All-World, which adds emerging markets. I read the factsheet, the top ten holdings, the country split and the number of constituents, because the label on the box rarely tells the whole story.

Next comes the replication method. Most large funds use full replication, buying every name in the index in proportion. Smaller or more awkward indices, such as small-cap or emerging-market ones, often use sampling, where the manager holds a representative subset. Sampling can be fine, but it widens tracking error, so I want to know which approach is used before I commit.

Fund size matters too. A very small fund carries closure risk; if assets drop below a workable level the provider may merge or shut it, which forces a sale and a fresh start elsewhere. I look for a fund that has run for at least five years with stable assets, and I check whether the provider has a habit of closing niche products.

Then there is the share class and the platform. The same index can be sold as an accumulating share class, which reinvests dividends inside the fund, or a distributing one, which pays them out. In a taxable account I usually prefer accumulating, since it spares me the job of reinvesting small payouts. On the platform side I compare dealing fees, any flat account charge and the spread I pay when buying.

Tracking difference is the honest measure. It takes the fund's return, subtracts the index return and shows what the wrapper cost me over a year, after fees, taxes on dividends and any securities lending. I look at the figure over three and five years, not just one, because a single year can flatter or punish a fund for reasons that will not repeat.

Securities lending is worth a glance. Many funds lend stock to earn a little extra, which can offset costs, but it adds counterparty risk. I do not avoid lenders outright; I prefer funds that keep the programme modest and split the revenue back to the fund.

I also care how long a fund has tracked its index without changing it. A provider that quietly swaps the benchmark, or reroutes a fund onto a cheaper index to cut costs, resets the history and can leave me holding something I never chose. I read the last few annual reports when I can, and I check that the name on the fund still matches the index inside it. A stable mandate is worth more to me than a slightly lower headline charge.

Currency and domicile catch people out. A fund listed in my own currency may still hold assets in others, and an unhedged share class will move with exchange rates. I accept that for long holds, but I want to know it is happening rather than assume the fund is somehow local. Domicile affects withholding tax on dividends, and the gap between an Irish-domiciled and a US-domiciled fund can quietly cost or save a chunk each year.

I also check the benchmark itself. A plain market-cap index is cheap to run; a strategy index that tilts to value or quality is really an active bet in disguise and will drift from the broad market. If I want a tilt I take it deliberately, not by accident.

Finally I look at the ongoing charge. For a plain index fund tracking a mainstream market, an expense ratio above 0.20% is a red flag; cheaper rivals usually exist for the same exposure, and the gap compounds for decades. That single number, read against the tracking difference, tells me most of what matters before I buy.

## Rebalancing

I check the split once a year, usually in January, and only act when a target drifts by more than five percentage points. A 5% band stops me fiddling for no reason. When a slice runs hot I bring it back by directing new contributions to the laggards first, and only sell if that is not enough. Selling inside a tax wrapper costs nothing; in a taxable account I weigh the capital gain against the tidier split. Annual is often enough, and the calendar reminder keeps me honest.
